05Exploring photo-based reporting

Could a photo do the describing for you?

We finished the Report a Problem and Customer Service forms earlier than expected, so in Sprint 5 we designed alternative ways to report a problem.

Concept

Image recognition is a concept, designed and tested as a Figma prototype. The recognition shown is simulated, not working functionality.

Exploration brief · Sprint 5

The brief

Sprint 4's plan included designing an artificial intelligence application to give users an alternative, more efficient way to report a problem. Sprint 5 set out to:

01

Research existing products that use machine learning and artificial intelligence to see whether there's an opportunity for a new Report a Problem solution.

02

Run lightning demos on alternative products.

03

Sketch new ideas.

04

Design new products.

Lightning demos

Purpose: find inspiring products, services, or experiences that could be adapted to DC Water's need for reporting water-related issues.

Standout examples included, but weren't limited to:

Waze
Real-time traffic reporting
Chipotle
Chatbot
Google Lens
 
Apple
Text support

Sketching and alternatives considered

The lightning demos triggered a wide range of ideas. The team brought them to DC Water, who voted for the ones they believed would meet users' needs while being logistically and financially feasible.

The team divided the work. I worked only on image recognition, so it's the only concept in this case study.

From sketch to wireframes

Sketch: the core idea in a single screen. Point the camera at the problem, let the product name the object (“Object Detected: Fire Hydrant”) with a short definition, then confirm or try again.

Wireframes: the team then wireframed the main screens of the image recognition design. They included a choice between form and camera, a camera view, problem details as a drawer or a full page, submission confirmation, and a ticket number.

Sketch for reporting a problem using image recognition.

Comparative testing · Sprint 5

Testing two directions for the landing and details screens

After the first iteration, we had different ideas for the interface and interactions, especially for the landing page and the problem details page. The team couldn't agree on the best options, so we tested both versions of each pair of screens with users.

6 participants, all of whom had tested the Report a Problem form. Goals: overall impressions of image recognition, and how it compares with the Report a Problem form for ease of use and effectiveness.

Landing page

Option A
Split button

Like the Report a Problem landing page, but “Report a Problem” splits into two buttons: fill out the traditional form or use image recognition.

Option B
Photo layout

Image recognition is the default. “Show us the issue” then offers image recognition or the traditional form. This assumed image recognition would be the easiest, most efficient option and that users would want to start with the fastest one.

Problem details

Option A
Interaction drawer

A drawer pattern we found in existing image recognition products. We liked its modern look but worried drawers are native to apps and might not translate well to responsive web pages.

Option B
Full page

A more classic layout, which we liked because the “Add Photo” button is very visible.

Wins
  • The photo layout landing page was simple and easy to use.
  • Users noticed and used the additional photo button on the full-page problem details layout.
  • The design met users' expectations about what would happen after uploading a photo.
  • Users appreciated the object descriptions after uploading a photo because they could learn the terminology while reporting.
  • Users liked that tags were selected automatically after uploading a photo, and appreciated being able to select more.
6 of 6participants said they'd prefer image recognition over the Report a Problem form (prototype preference)
Opportunities
  • The “Image Identifier” label on the split-button landing page confused some users, who didn't know what to expect.
  • Users were unlikely to close the drawer on the problem details page unless they wanted a full view of their image.
  • Users didn't notice the additional photo button in the drawer layout.
  • Users found the confirmation message after selecting “Submit” unnecessary.
  • Users didn't know how to save the ticket number after submitting.
Iteration 2 · Sprint 5

Revisions after testing

Submitting and tracking without a ticket number

What we learned

The confirmation message after “Submit” felt unnecessary, and users didn't know how to save the ticket number.

↓
What changed

The extra submit step was removed: users get a thank-you message and can exit right away. The copy-ticket-number option was removed, and users track their report by uploading the original photo.

Landing page and problem details layouts

What we learned

The photo layout landing page was simple and easy to use, while “Image Identifier” confused some users. Users noticed the additional photo button on the full-page layout but not in the drawer.

↓
What the final screens show

The final prototype uses the photo layout landing page (“Show Us The Issue”) and the full-page problem details, where users can add another photo.

Final landing
Additional photo uploaded

Other additions in the second iteration

Error

A message when an uploaded photo isn't recognized as an eligible DC Water object.

Form option

“No photo? Fill out a form.” sends users to the Report a Problem form when image recognition isn't suitable.

Object outline

A label and an outline around the object make it easy to identify.

Location

Users can edit their location if the detected location is inaccurate.
